gloss: it seems; it appears; it looks like

definitions.gloss: it seems; it appears; it looks like
definitions.explanation: Expresses the speaker's judgment or inference based on what they have observed or sensed. Indicates that something appears to be a certain way.
Used to make comparisons or similes, expressing that something resembles or is similar to something else.

definitions.gloss: in such a way that; so that
definitions.explanation: Used with verbs to express a desired manner or goal, indicating the way something should be done.

examples.english: It looks like it's going to rain.

examples.japanese: {彼|かれ}は{疲|つか}れているようだ。
{話|はなし}の{内容|ないよう}から{判断|はんだん}すると、{彼女|かのじょ}は{転職|てんしょく}を{考|かんが}えているようだ。
examples.english: Judging from what she said, it seems she's considering changing jobs.

examples.japanese: {夢|ゆめ}を{見|み}ているようだった。
examples.english: It was as if I were dreaming.

examples.japanese: {子供|こども}でも{分|わ}かるように{説明|せつめい}してください。
examples.english: Please explain it so that even a child can understand.

examples.japanese: {忘|わす}れないように{手帳|てちょう}に{書|か}いておく。
examples.english: I'll write it in my planner so I don't forget.

examples.japanese: {風邪|かぜ}を{引|ひ}かないように{気|き}をつけてね。
examples.english: Be careful not to catch a cold.

examples.japanese: {合格|ごうかく}できるように{毎日|まいにち}{練習|れんしゅう}している。
examples.english: I practice every day so that I can pass.

notes:
One of the most versatile and frequently used expressions in Japanese. Written as {様|よう}だ when using kanji, though the hiragana form is more common. Attaches to the plain form of verbs, い-adjectives, な-adjective stems + な, and nouns + の.

COMMON PATTERNS:
- verb plain + ようだ: {来|く}るようだ (it seems they're coming)
- い-adjective + ようだ: {寒|さむ}いようだ (it seems cold)
- な-adjective + なようだ: {元気|げんき}なようだ (seems healthy)
- noun + のようだ: {春|はる}のようだ (like spring)
- ように + verb: {聞|き}こえるように{話|はな}す (speak so one can be heard)
- ようにする: to make an effort to; to make sure to
- ようになる: to come to; to become able to

SIMILAR WORDS:
- みたいだ: colloquial equivalent of ようだ (sense 1 and 2); ようだ is more formal
- らしい: based on hearsay or indirect evidence, while ようだ is based on the speaker's own observation
- そうだ (appearance): based on visual impression of the moment, while ようだ involves more deliberate judgment
